prime.problem: Largest Rectangle in Histogram asks, for every bar, how far it can stretch left and right before a shorter bar stops it. Trying every pair of walls is 50,005,000 pairs at n = 10⁴; expanding from each bar is O(n²) on sorted input.
prime.fits: Follows the parsing stack: same push and pop, but now the pops are triggered by comparing values rather than matching brackets. It is the one-sided cousin of the monotonic deque, and it uses the same each-index-once argument from the Big-O card.
expect: a stack of indices whose heights never drop
right wall: the bar that triggers the pop
left wall: the index under the popped one
sentinels: an appended 0 and a −1 at the bottom
next smaller / next greater element as the general pattern
prime.goal: Find, for every element, its nearest smaller neighbour on both sides in one O(n) pass, and use it to solve Largest Rectangle in Histogram.

attend: At the moment a bar is popped, why are both of its walls known?
Why is the width i − new top − 1 and not i − top?
What does the appended 0 do, and what breaks without it?
Why does the −1 at the bottom never get popped?
Which direction of monotonicity finds the next smaller element, and which the next greater?

must: Heights on the stack never drop → a shorter bar i arrives → it is the first shorter bar to the right of every taller bar on top → the index beneath each popped bar is the first shorter bar to its left → both walls known → area = h × (i − new top − 1) → pop and forget
Each index is pushed once and popped at most once → the inner while totals ≤ n pops over the whole pass → O(n), at most 2n + 1 stack operations (≤ 20,001 at n = 10⁴ vs 50,005,000 pairs)
Sentinel 0 appended at the end → every leftover bar gets popped and scored → the −1 at the bottom reads h[−1] = that same 0, which nothing is shorter than → no empty-stack checks
elevated: Pop only strictly taller bars (x < h[top]) → equal bars stay stacked → an earlier equal bar is scored with too small a width, but the last equal bar popped spans the whole run → the maximum is still right
reference: Reconstruct Itinerary being filed under Stacks in the source (it is Hierholzer's algorithm)
the list of further uses (daily temperatures, trapping rain water, maximal rectangle)
the divide-at-minimum O(n log n) alternative

compress.prompt: From memory, draw heights [2, 1, 5, 6, 2, 3] and the stack at i = 4, and mark the two walls of the bar that scores 10. Then explain in 3 sentences why the whole pass is O(n).
checklist: stack holds indices with non-decreasing heights
the arriving shorter bar is the right wall; the index underneath is the left wall
at i = 4: pop 6 (width 1, area 6), pop 5 (width 4 − 1 − 1 = 2, area 10)
sentinels flush the stack and remove the empty-stack case
each index pushed once, popped at most once

retrieve.q: Explain why the bar on top of the stack can be scored the instant a shorter bar arrives, and never later.
answer: the arriving bar is the first shorter bar to its right: its right wall
everything between it and the bar below it on the stack was at least as tall (those were popped earlier), so the bar below is its left wall
its widest rectangle is now fixed, so it can be popped and forgotten

retrieve.q: Walk through the sentinel step i = 6 for heights [2, 1, 5, 6, 2, 3] with the stack holding indices −1, 1, 4, 5.
answer: stops at −1 because h[−1] is the 0 itself; best stays 10

retrieve.q: Why not split at the minimum bar recursively (best of min × width, left part, right part)? What would you need to make it safe?
answer: it is O(n log n) with balanced splits
on sorted input each split peels off one bar: O(n²)
a range-minimum structure (segment tree or sparse table) makes finding the minimum fast, but the stack is simpler and always O(n)

compare.q: Both keep indices in sorted value order. What does a pop mean in each, and why does the deque need a second exit?
answer: stack pop: the popped bar has found its next smaller element (its right wall)
deque back pop: the popped value can never again be the window max
the deque also expires the front because the window slides; the histogram has no expiry
both are O(n) because each index enters and leaves once

compare.q: The parsing stack pops on a matching closer; this stack pops on a smaller value. What does each stack's content mean at any moment?
answer: parsing: the open contexts, innermost on top
monotonic: bars still waiting for a shorter bar on their right, in increasing height
both push and pop each item once: O(n)
parsing depth follows nesting; monotonic depth reaches n + 1 on ascending input

predict.q: Run the algorithm on [2, 2, 2]. Before tracing: which bars get popped with the wrong (too small) width, and is the final answer still right?
predict.answer: The first two bars are scored with widths 1 and 2 (areas 2 and 4) because equal bars aren't popped until the sentinel, and each pop sees an equal bar, not a shorter one, underneath. The last one popped reaches the −1 marker with width 3, area 6, which is correct. The maximum is right because the last bar of any run of equal heights always gets the full width.

apply.task: Trace largest_rectangle([6, 2, 5, 4, 5, 1, 6]) by hand as the card does: the stack after each step and every pop's area. Count pushes and pops.
apply.done: You find the answer 12 (height 4, width 3, popped at i = 5 with walls at indices 1 and 5), with 8 pushes and 7 pops, including the sentinel.
apply.hint: At i = 5 (h 1) four bars are popped in one step.

reflect: Which prediction did you get wrong: which equal bars were under-scored, or whether the answer survived?
Could you explain the width formula with a picture of the two walls?
Which relationship is still fuzzy: pop trigger → right wall, or index beneath → left wall?
Which of the listed uses (daily temperatures, trapping rain water, sum of subarray minimums) could you now write?
When would you reach for the monotonic deque instead?
